Best Nintendo 64 (N64) Emulator: Mupen64Plus Platforms: Windows, macOS, Linux, Android Alternatives: Project64

If you're looking to play Super Mario 64 or GoldenEye for the Nintendo 64, look no further than Mupen64Plus. This emulator supports save states, take screenshots, and has built-in cheats. Keyboard shortcuts are supported for multiple system functions. Advanced features like online play and graphic enhancements like anti-aliasing and VSync are also included.

Download and install the program from GitHub https://github.com/mupen64plus (or Google Play for Android), https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=paulscode.android.mupen64plus.free&hl=en_US and it's ready to go—no complex run commands required and no interface plug-in necessary. ROMs won't be stored inside the GUI, so it's a good idea to arrange your games in one centralized location for easy access. By default, Mupen64Plus assigns all input to your keyboard, but you can also connect up to four controllers.

Best Multi-System Emulator for PC: RetroArch Platforms: Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android Alternatives: OpenEmu (for macOS)

For PC gamers, RetroArch(Opens in a new window) is like the holy grail of emulation. This all-in-one front end uses the libretro API to support cores for multiple systems, with an immense selection of configurations to fully customize gameplay elements and video/audio settings. However, RetroArch lacks a user friendly setup scheme, requiring you to download individual cores and select which you want to use before booting up a game.

As an emulator, RetroArch supports an impressive number of systems, including Atari, DS, Game Boy, GameCube, MAME, NES, Nintendo 64, PlayStation, SNES, Wii, and more. The front end supports basic features like save states, screen filters, screenshots and video recording, and controller and hotkey customization. More advanced features include netplay, custom achievements, rewind, fast-forward, and slow motion, user interface customization, and built-in streaming.

Graphical settings allow you to adjust refresh rate, display resolution, aspect ratio, VSync, anti-latency, anti-aliasing, and anti-ghosting features. RetroArch also gives you full control over audio controls and sound mixing. For basic setup or advanced configurations, reference the libretro documentation(Opens in a new window).

Best Multi-System Emulator for Microconsoles: RetroPie

If you prefer not to be stuck on a computer, you can build a classic game system for cheap with a Raspberry Pi board and an operating system to run it. This is where RetroPie(Opens in a new window) comes in; it's a free Linux distribution based on Raspbian and combines LibRetro's RetroArch API with the EmulationStation front end. Other items you will need include an SD card for games, case, power source, and controller.

Similar to other multi-system emulators, RetroPie supports a laundry list of consoles(Opens in a new window), and once your new microconsole is built, everything should be good to go. We have a guide to help you through the setup process.

Best Super Nintendo Emulator: Snes9x Platforms: Windows, macOS, Linux, Android Alternatives: bsnes(Opens in a new window), bsnes-hd

Snes9x is the best emulator for Super Nintendo and Super Famicom games. Download the program from one of the sites the developers link to on the Downloads page to get started. An open-source port called Snes9x EV+ is available for Android devices.

You will find that Snes9x supports multiple save slots, multicart emulation, cheat codes, and ROM hacks. The emulator also allows you to tweak frame rate and sound, take screenshots and video, and play online through built-in netplay.

When it comes to game input, you can customize your hotkeys or connect a controller. Snes9x can emulate the original Super Nintendo controller, as well as the Super NES Mouse, Super Scope, and other peripherals.

S for Sync Joy-Con controller (aka, pair, authorize, connect and configure each – when not attached)

[source: https://www.techradar.com/reviews/nintendo-switch

Console needs to be told whether Joy-Cons are being used together or separately

Pairing the controllers is a little more complicated than with other devices because of the fact that they can either be paired or used separately. The way you tell the Switch which controllers you're using is to press both the L and R shoulder buttons in whichever configuration you've opted for. So if you're using the Joy-Cons individually, you press the buttons on the Joy-Con straps to indicate this is the case.]

The SL + SR sync buttons, short-pressed, together, both at the same time, are only used when the Joy-Con mini-controller is not attached to the Grip (or the Switch console for hand-held use) but rather will be used as an independent mini-controller in the horizontal orientation for Table-top use or with the console in the docking stand and connected to a home TV, and when the Switch console main menu Controller option is being displayed (see the picture below), and used to determine:

1 – Will just one person (a single-player) be playing (and controlling the game as Player 1, aka, P1)?

2 – If so, which Joy-Con will he or she use, and is that Joy-Con added, authorized, connected and configured by the Switch console for horizontal use (with a game that supports an independent Joy-Con mini-controller ([which, yes, our 3 Mario games just so happen to; so, thank you, very kindly, for asking about that] and rather than as a traditional [Pro] controller, whether using an actual Nintendo Pro Controller or a set of Left and Right Joy-Cons attached to a Joy-Con Grip or not [but being used as a single set, as if they were attached to a Grip, aka, Dual Joy-Con])?

Those first two questions are all answered by Player 1 (P1 or a supervisor) short pressing both the SL + SR sync buttons at the same time on a Right Joy-Con controller (or the L + R top shoulder-buttons when using Dual Joy-Con, that is, a set of Joy-Cons attached to a Joy-Con Grip for normal, quasi-traditional controller use because "price is no object" NOT, that is, each separate traditional [Pro-quality] controller costs half again as much as the whole Switch and two (Joy-Con mini-) controllers are already included with every Switch). Pressing those keys adds that Joy-Con to the Console Controller Setup screen, configures it for horizontal use and as Controller 1. (The Controller 1 designation is important if more than one controller should subsequently be added, because it controls the ⌂ Home button function as well as the options for Player 1 [P1] which may set the tone for anyone watching or who may later want to be added in to play co-operatively with P1). And, as the Console Controller Setup screen indicates (see the picture below), P1 (or a supervisor) after adding Controller 1, must also then press the A / ▸ Right (Directional) Face button (actually the A button because there is no ▸ Right button on a Right Joy-Con and the A button also serves as the ▸ Right Directional button when the Joy-Con is used horizontally) on P1's Joy-Con to indicate that P1 has checked his or her controller setup (and specifically that the 1 green light on P1's Joy-Con's "Player LED" lights and the 1 green light in the Console Controller Setup screen's on-screen representation of P1's controller both agree and together indicate that Player 1's Joy-Con is added, connected, configured for horizontal use and as the Controller 1) and therefore Player 1 is all added, configured, set and ready to proceed and go on to whatever may happen next.

3 – If the answer to question 1 above was not "yes" (that is, more than one person wants to play a game that supports multiplayer mode), then first add Player 1 as per above, and then ask: who has a second (Left Joy-Con mini-) controller and wants to be added as Player 2, aka, P2 to the Console Controller Setup screen with his or her controller configured as Controller 2 and as an individual Joy-Con mini-controller for independent, horizontal use (to be used separately, stand-alone, and apart from a Right Joy-Con rather than as a traditional [Pro] controller [Dual Joy-Con attached to a Grip]? Pressing the SL + SR sync buttons together on a Left mini-controller would answer that, and pressing the A / ▸ Right (Directional) Face button (actually there is no A button and the ▸ Right Directional button functions exactly as an A button when the Right Joy-Con is configured and used horizontally) on Player 2's Left Joy-Con indicates that P2 (or someone responsible) has checked P2's controller setup (and specifically that the 2 green lights on P2's Joy-Con and the 2 green lights in the Console Controller Setup's on-screen representation of P2's controller both came on and agree and together indicate that Player 2's Left Joy-Con is added, connected, configured for horizontal use and as Controller 2 in that screen) and that therefore Player 2 is all added, connected, configured, set and ready to proceed and go on to whatever may happen next, and a press of the A / ▸ Right Directional Face button on P2's Left Joy-Con confirms all that (P1 or a supervisor may press the buttons for P2 on Controller 2 if that would help things to proceed more quickly to the surprisingly new and exciting parts of playing awesome Switch games like Super Mario, Kart or Odyssey!).

4 – Is there a Player 3 with a second Right Joy-Con mini-controller for use as Controller 3?

5 – Is there a Player 4 with a second Left Joy-Con mini-controller for use as Controller 4?

For each of those last two questions, Question 4 and Question 5, is that Player's separate controller properly added, connected and configured, whether as a Joy-Con mini-controller for horizonal use, or as a traditional (Pro) controller; if the former, that is indicated by pressing both the SL + SR sync buttons at the same time on a different, not yet registered (nor connected on this Console Controller Setup screen session as another, just now added, Joy-Con mini-controller), and, like in Question 3, and, one at a time, another Player (or Player 1 or a responsible supervisor) goes through the same process again, and the next Player (or P1 or a responsible supervisor) can confirm each step, both on-screen in the Console Controller Setup screen (see a picture of that screen below), and on each, separate, physical (Joy-Con mini-) controller as it is individually added to the Console Controller Setup screen. Specifically, for Player 3, do the 3 green LED Player lights come on, on the actual controller and on the picture representing that Controller 3 in the Controller Setup screen such that both agree and thereby indicate that the Controller 3 is properly added (aka, registered / authorized / paired), connected via Bluetooth 3.0 to the Console Controller Setup screen, configured for horizontal use and as Controller 3 for use by P3? Or, for Player 4, are 4 green LED lights on, both on-screen and on the physical Controller 4, which together would indicate that Controller 4 has been properly added, configured for horizontal use by P4? And then, subsequently to that LED light count agreement check, the A / ▸ Right (Directional) Face on that next controller which was most recently added to the Console Controller Setup screen must be pressed, the Console Controller Setup screen can proceed and together all Players can go on to whatever may happen next. (What happens next may be that Player 1's Controller 1 is used to exit the Console Controller Setup screen [by pressing his A / ▸ Right Directional Face button a second time] and P1 would then be able proceed to [re-]start or continue the actual game whose card is inserted into the Switch console game card slot [since no more Players need to be added to the Console Controller Setup screen]; or, another Player (P2 up to P4) may take his or her turn to press the SL + SR buttons on another Joy-Con to add, connect, configure it on the Console Controller setup screen; or whatever else that may need to happen.

Note also, in the screenshot picture below, that the Console Controller Setup screen instructs the user to press the L + R top shoulder-buttons but then colors the specified buttons blue and then shows separate pictures above at the top of that screen, of each of the two, possible Joy-Con configurations and exactly which buttons L + R would mean for each of those 2 cases and in Case 3. In Case 1 – (the recommended, as in "price is no object" case, especially for single-player, but also for any multiplayer mode) when a set of Joy-Cons are attached to a Joy-Con Grip, then, literally use the L top shoulder-button (aka, Left Bumper) on the Left Joy-Con together short pressed down together with the R top shoulder-button (aka, Right Bumper) on the Right Joy-Con, both at the same time; Case 2 – when one to four Joy-Con mini-controllers will be used horizontally by the same number of players, then use the SL + SR buttons on a single Joy-Con to, one at a time, add each of those (mini-) controllers; or, Case 3 – when a Player wants to be added and use a traditional controller, then also use the L + R top shoulder-buttons (Left + Right Bumpers) on his or her controller; and, when done syncing any controller, press the A / ▸ Right (Directional) Face button (or either one in Case 3) to indicate that that controller is showing the same number of Player green LED lights as the picture indicates, that that Player is finished adding and configuring the Console Controller Setup screen and ready so that either that screen can exit or another Player can take his turn to be added; but if a Player is not finished, then as the screen shows, that Player on his or her controller [or another Player already added?] can press his or her - / + button which will ask the Console to try again to connect, or pressing and holding that button will ask the Console to search for (and re-pair its Bluetooth-based detection, registration and authorization of) that controller; or short pressing the Down (Directional) Face button (or the B / ▸ Right button?, or whichever button that that Console Controller Setup screen says to use, which may change depending on the type of controller: horizontal Joy-Con, a set of Joy-Cons attached to a Grip, or an actual traditional controller) in order to go back out (of this process of trying to get this particular controller added to the Console Controller Setup) so something else can happen.

Keep it simple, but not too simple: Five views of the Dual Joy-Con set, which set may consist of a blue and a red one – Grampa calls the 5 views: Top, Front, Side, Back and End.

Important: The Nintendo Switch console must be connected online to download a system update.

Note: In most situations, the Nintendo Switch will automatically download the most recent system update. Use the following steps if you wish to manually start the update process. If you are unable to perform the system update, restart your console and try again.

Complete these steps

Select the System Settings on the HOME Menu.

System Settings being highlighted on the Nintendo Switch HOME Menu Screen

Scroll down through the System Settings menu and select System.

Select System Update, to start the system update process.

During the process, the system will first perform a check to determine if a new system update is available. If an update is available, the download process will begin automatically.

Ensuring that your Nintendo Switch is completely up-to-date is a good way to avoid any issues.

The same goes for your Nintendo Switch's Joy-Cons, though updating your controllers is slightly different from the console itself.

First attach a pair of Joy-Cons directly to the Console itself

From your Nintendo Switch's home menu, navigate to System Settings at the bottom of your screen.

Within System Settings, scroll down the left-hand side options until you find Controllers and Sensors.

Enter the options for Controllers and Sensors and you should see each individual option for your Joy-Cons. Scroll down until you find Update Controllers.

Select Update Controllers and your Nintendo Switch will begin updating each Joy-Con attached to the console itself.

Remove that set of Joy-Cons from the Console, attach the second pair and repeat the steps above.

Update Controllers being highlighted within the system option in the System Settings

The Joy-Con can be paired to the Nintendo Switch console in the following ways:

Joint pairing Simply attach the Joy-Con controllers to the console.

1--Button pairing or wireless pairing From the HOME Menu, select Controllers from the icons at the bottom, then select Change Grip and Order. While the following screen is displayed, press and hold down the SYNC Button for at least one second on the controller you wish to pair. Once paired, - you'll feel it rumble to confirm the link and the player LED(s) corresponding to the controller number will remain lit.

2--Confirm how the Joy-Con will be held.

Important

By doing the Button Pairing alone, the console will not be able to tell if the Joy-Con will be held as a dual-controller grip, or if the Joy-Con will be held horizontally as individual controllers.

To confirm how the Joy-Con will be used, press the L Button/R Buttons as indicated below while on this screen.

How to Use the Joy-Con

Buttons to Press

As a dual-controller grip

Joy-Con controllers used as a dual-controller grip

Buttons to Press

L Button (on left Joy-Con) + R Button (on right Joy-Con)

ZL Button (on left Joy-Con) + ZR Button (on right Joy-Con)

As a solo horizontal grip

Joy-Con controller used as a solo horizontal grip

Buttons to Press

SL Button + SR Button on each Joy-Con you wish to use horizontally

Once the controllers are linked appropriately, press 'A' (or the button on the right of the diamond if you're using a single Joy-Con - either the 'right' D-button or 'X') and you're ready to go.

If the controllers link incorrectly, simply tap 'B' (or the 'down' D-button/'A' on a single Joy-Con) to return to the previous screen and then hit 'Change Grip/Order' again to return and retry.

You can sync up to eight Nintendo Switch controllers to a single Nintendo Switch.

You can play using the Joy-Con controllers as one unit, as two separate controllers, or you can use the Nintendo Switch Pro Controller.

There are also special controller hubs, which often require their own separate accessories to sync with your Switch. This means four pairs of Joy-Cons (or eight if you're playing them individually), and up to two controller hubs (each of which supports four controllers, again adding up to eight).

Note: The only exceptions here are if you're using Nintendo Pro Controllers — only four can connect at once — or if you've connected Bluetooth headphones to your Switch. While Bluetooth headphones are connected, you can only use two wireless controllers (or one pair of Joy-Cons).

How to sync Nintendo Switch controllers with your system, so that up to eight people can play at once

Written by Steven John and William Antonelli Updated Sep 15, 2021, 2:38 PM

To sync a Nintendo Switch controller, you'll need to go into the "Change Grip/Order" menu.

You can sync up to eight Nintendo Switch controllers to a single Nintendo Switch.

There are also special controller hubs, which often require their own separate accessories to sync with your Switch.

When it comes to Nintendo Switch games, the more the merrier. Multiplayer gaming only enhances the fun, especially when you and your friends or family are playing together in the same room.

A Switch console can support up to eight controllers connected at the same time. This means four pairs of Joy-Cons (or eight if you're playing them individually), and up to two controller hubs (each of which supports four controllers, again adding up to eight).

Note: The only exceptions here are if you're using Nintendo Pro Controllers — only four can connect at once — or if you've connected Bluetooth headphones to your Switch. While Bluetooth headphones are connected, you can only use two wireless controllers (or one pair of Joy-Cons).

Once you've got your controllers, here's how to sync them.

How to sync a Nintendo Switch controller with your console The best way to sync a Nintendo Switch controller will depend on what sort of controller you have.

The easiest way to sync a pair of Joy-Con controllers to a Nintendo Switch is simply to slide them onto the physical console. The right- and left-hand Joy-Con controller will then be linked to that Nintendo Switch until affixed to a different console, or until the remote pairing steps below are followed.

You can also sync a Pro Controller by connecting it to your Switch's dock with a USB-C cable.

To pair controllers remotely:

1. From the Switch's homepage, scroll down to the "Controllers" tab — it looks like a single gray Joy-Con — and click it.

2. Select "Change Grip/Order."

3. If you're trying to pair a new controller or Joy-Con, you'll want to press and hold its SYNC button (a small circular button, usually on the top) for about five seconds before moving on to the next steps.

4. If you want to use a Joy-Con (or multiple Joy-Cons) as an individual controller, take it out of the Switch and press both its shoulder buttons at the same time — they're labeled "SL" and "SR." It may take a few presses for the Switch to recognize them.

5. If you want to use two Joy-Cons as a single controller, press the shoulder buttons on each Joy-Con at the same time. They're labeled "ZL" and "ZR." You can add up to four Joy-Con pairs.

6. If you want to pair a Pro Controller, press its shoulder buttons, "ZL" and "ZR," at the same time.

If a controller that worked before won't sync, press the SYNC button anyway (again, the small circular button). Your Switch may have forgotten the controller and needs to be reminded of it again.

If you're using a controller hub, just connect the hub to your Switch's dock via USB and plug your controllers into the hub. They should work automatically.

A Right Joy-Con also weights just under 3 grams more than a Left one partly because it has a NFC / amiibo reader under its joy stick, whereby one can purchase Toys-to-Life / interactive gaming figures specifically, for example, to permanently unlock Kart racing suits for Players customed designed with Mii, based on the character scanned. Both Joy-Cons also have motion detection build-in, including an accelerometer and gyroscope, and which are used in Kart's tilt controls, for example. However, only the Right Joy-Con has a tiny IR (infrared) Motion camera on the opposite shoulder from its 2 shoulder buttons and near the ⌂ Home button (which may also partly explain why it's just under 3 grams heavier than a Left Joy-Con) and that can detect and track depth and read an object's shape and motions, for example, which shape a player's hand is signing (rock, paper or scissors.) But, other than waking up the Switch console with the ⌂ Home button while pointing the IR camera at the console (must be direct line of sight without anything blocking the infrared light), the IR camera is perhaps mainly used with the Leg Strap accessory for Switch Sports Football, aka Soccer, matches.

Both Joy-Cons also have the most dynamic "HD rumble" or haptic feedback engine of any controller to date, which make it "imitate the feel of individual ice cubes and water being poured into a glass" or like there's a speaker in each Joy-Con that makes your fingers sense fine tactile feedback and you feel immersed in explosions and earthquakes in games, or, for example the rumbling motor scooters in Odyssey's Metro Kingdom.

For any controller that is currently paired and whose battery is not depleted, from the Console Controllers Setup menu off the Home screen it's possible to find a misplaced controller by tapping or selecting the controller's icon, causing the paired controller to vibrate loudly.

providing the Switch console with a Joy-Con controller that also doubles as two individual controllers is a very neat inclusion, and should mean that you're always able to join a friend for a quick multiplayer game while you're out and about.

[source: https://www.techradar.com/reviews/nintendo-switch

The phrase "jack of all trades and master of none" may sound negative, but the impression the Nintendo Switch has left us with is that sometimes compromise is necessary and good.

Yes there are better home consoles out there with controllers that can be good at doing just one thing, and yes there are handhelds out there that have better battery life and a more compact form-factor, but no other piece of gaming hardware has attempted the sheer number of things as the Nintendo Switch does – and then delivered so competently on so many of them.

The graphics aren't the best around, but they're good enough that they don't feel dated. The controller isn't the most comfortable, but it never feels outright difficult to use. The battery life isn't the best, but it's enough for daily use.

All of these trade-offs have been born out of compromise and an attempt to make something that works in so many situations, and on that final point the Nintendo Switch is a great success.

What remains to be seen is if, in the years ahead, its games library can shape up to be something you'll want to play both at home and on the go, and whether its online service can compete with the existing efforts from Sony and Microsoft. If both of these play out well, Nintendo will have found a set of compromises worth making.

By trying to do many things at once the Joy-Cons don't do anything perfectly: the buttons are oddly positioned due to having to work as a combined controller.

Let's not forget Nintendo has designed some absolutely classic controllers in its time – the original NES controller wrote the blueprint that console controllers have followed ever since, the N64 was the first console to have a controller with an analogue thumb-stick, and the Wii (for better or for worse) introduced the world to motion-controlled gaming.

With the Nintendo Switch, Nintendo has attempted the seemingly impossible in creating a system that's simultaneously one whole controller and two separate controllers, while also functioning as controllers in the handheld mode.

Ultimately these multiple roles mean the Nintendo Switch controllers end up being jacks of all trades and masters of none. None of the controller configurations are unusable, but we've used more comfortable controllers in the past that have had the advantage of only having to do one job very well.

The right Joy-Con has an oddly and slightly awkwardly placed right analogue stick: placed underneath the face buttons, while the left Joy-Con's D-pad sums up the problem in a nutshell: rather than going for the cross D-pad that Nintendo has been using since the NES, the D-pad is instead split into four separate buttons to allow them to be used as face buttons when the Joy-Con is utilized as an individual controller. The result is a D-pad that you're not going to want to use for classic games that rely on it a lot, such as Street Fighter.

The Nintendo Switch analogue sticks also feel like a compromise between form factors: too small for a traditional gamepad, yet big enough that we wouldn't want to throw the device too carelessly into a rucksack for fear of one of them snapping off.

One part of the Switch controllers that we absolutely love are the face buttons. They're a little smaller than those on other consoles, but they've got a really satisfying click to them that we really appreciate.

It's in the handheld configuration that the Nintendo Switch controller's deficiencies are most apparent. The main problem is the low positioning of the right analogue stick, which we found very difficult to operate comfortably.

Either you hold the Switch precariously on the tips of your fingers in order to operate the analogue stick with the tip of your right thumb, or you hold the device more tightly and operate the thumbstick with the inside of your thumb knuckle, which feels rather cramped and awkward.

The weight of the Nintendo Switch makes it more difficult to comfortably hold on the fingertips. It's a mode that we think works in small bursts, but it's not comfortable over longer periods.

If you're gaming on Nintendo Switch on a flight, for example, we'd expect most people to opt to put the console in tabletop mode on the tray table in front of them. We are, however, fans of the shoulder buttons, which manage to feel big enough without impacting on the depth of the console too much.

We were surprised with how the Nintendo Switch controller feels when assembled in the grip.

Although the analogue sticks are a little small, we found them perfectly usable for lengthy Breath of the Wild play sessions, and the addition of a little more plastic massively helps the ergonomics of the controller as a whole.

It's just a shame that the controller doesn’t have a proper D-pad on its left side: as it stands you're going to need to buy the Pro controller if you want that traditional Nintendo controller feel on the Nintendo Switch.

]

The first half of the 16 play buttons are on the Right Joy-Con mini-controller while the second half are on the Left one.

Right Joy-Con mini-controller — these Basic 8 are used exactly the same on the Left mini-controller when configured for horizontal (aka, sideways) use

The 4 (Right Joy-Con) Face Buttons

A, B, X, Y

The 2 (Right Joy-Con) Shoulder buttons

R (shoulder Bumper), ZR (back-behind shoulder Trigger)

+, Right Stick

The + button is the equivalent of the Wii U's 'Start' button and may be used with the same meaning as the - button and either used to pause the game (in Kart, for example) or to access menus

The Right Stick is clickable as well as functioning as an analog, tilt joystick, control stick or thumbstick (analog means that the degree of tilt makes a difference just like a gas pedal on a vehicle plus, whereas digital joysticks only allow the four "cardinal" directions (up, right, left, down) or perhaps those plus 4 diagonal ones, analog sticks allow inputs in "all" directions ("360" directions) and map the full range of motion of the stick)

Left Joy-Con mini-controller – Advanced 8 — only used for Dual Joy-Con (i.e., when configured in the Console Controller Setup screen for use vertically, as a set with a Right Joy-Con, whether attached to a Grip or not.)

[source: https://www.techradar.com/reviews/nintendo-switch/2

On the left Joy-Con the D-pad/face buttons are in the centre of the controller, which means your right thumb is uncomfortably far over, and the same is true of the analogue stick on the right Joy-Con. The asymmetrical configuration also makes describing controls to another person very difficult, since the control buttons have different names between the two Joy-Cons.

The lack of hand grips is also prone to causing cramp if you use the controllers over long periods, especially if the game you're playing relies heavily on the Joy-Con's shoulder buttons. As a final point, the shoulder buttons can feel a little stiff to press, which adds to the discomfort of using them over long periods.

So while this configuration might work in a pinch if you want to let a friend join you for a couple of rounds of Mario Kart, we don't see it being something you'll want to spend a lot of time with. Additionally, you'll need to remember to carry the Joy-Con straps with your Nintendo Switch if you want to use the shoulder buttons, which will be an annoying inconvenience for most people.

Alternatively, you can use the two Joy-Cons as a single controller while split apart. Here they function identically to when they’re assembled into the Joy-Con grip, although we found it much less comfortable because of how cramped the right analogue stick ends up feeling.

Again, this feels like a compromise, this time for when you've forgotten your Joy-Con grip. We can't see ourselves using this configuration much at all unless a motion-controlled game specifically calls for it in the future.

The Left Stick functions just like the Right Stick in most 2D or 2.5D side-scrolling platform games (like Super Mario, Legend of Zelda, Sim City 2000, where 2.5D means that the game Player character action can only be to move up, right, left or down in a single [aka, 2D] plane, even though it seems as if you see [from the camera's perceived] depth of field that things are crossing from the foreground to the background and back – seemingly into and out of the 2D plane with different [camera] perspective angles) – which makes the gameplay more engaging and more immersive.

However, in some 2.5D games like Odyssey, the Left Stick may control the Player's 2D movement while the Right Stick may control the camera's "3D" view of the action, and, depending on the game, one may suppose that both may be able to be controlled independently (and simultaneously, if the game supports that).

2.5D versus 3D

What follows below is minor digression, diversion or side note about 2.5D versus 3D (in video games and graphics)

While a display system effect that included rotation and scaling and allowed for a 3D effect while moving in any direction without any actual 3D models was used to simulate 3D graphics on the SNES, all Switch graphics are 2.5D game graphics. Earlier 2.5D was composed of objects represented by two-dimensional images applied to a single polygon which was typically kept perpendicular to the line of sight, but with special light and texture, while the rest of the scene may have had 3D linear perspectives that combine the visibility and mobility of a top-down game with the character recognizability of a side-scrolling game, the player is presented an overview of the game world in the ability to see it from above, more or less, and with additional details in artwork made possible by using an angle.

Instead of showing a Player character in top-down perspective, as a head and shoulders seen from above, the entire body was drawn when using a slanted angle; turning a character around would reveal how it looks from the sides, the front and the back, while the top-down perspective would display the same head and shoulders regardless. Early examples include Super Mario Kart and Super Mario 64. But later "3D" game graphics while including one to three sets of parallels defining one to three vanishing points can perhaps even include 3D character models based off of a poly 3D mesh (with a specific max polygon count of the model that would be much less than the several thousand polygons per second of a true 3D character such as Golum in "The Lord of the Rings"), but still, typically only include 2D plane character action, mimicking real-world action on flat, 2D surfaces with the impression of drawing objects on canvas that appears to be in a 3D view by using shadows, layering, perspective graphics, parallax scrolling (in Super Mario World) and other techniques to create a change in depth that deceives us into seeing 3-D graphics.

Real 3D Player action from a worm's eye view or a bird's eye view would actually become too messy to see, understand, control or think through strategically 100% of the action time – true 3D character action using curvilinear, fisheye perspective (like a vehicle's back-up camera that distorts all the edges) with four, five or more vanishing points (four in a circle, named N, W, E, S, plus a fifth in the center, in computer animation and motion graphics is called tiny planet) or the stylized curvilinear inverse of that, as seen in cartoon graphics, even if a person's real, round eyes can imagine it, is actually something that not even a wide-angle, rectilinear lens camera can capture, because objects still appear increasingly stretched and enlarged as they near the edge of the frame.

The best "3D-action" games that may sometimes permit 3D-like Player movement include the (2011) Super Mario Kart 7, The (2011) Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time 3D, the (2011) Ghost Recon: Shadow Wars; the (2012) New Super Mario Bros. 2, the (2012) Animal Crossing: New Leaf, the (2012) Star Fox 64 3D, the (2012) Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater 3D, The (2013) Legend of Zelda: A Link Between Worlds, the (2013) Donkey Kong Country Returns 3D, the (2013) Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney - Dual Destinies, the (2014) Kirby: Triple Deluxe, the (2017) Fire Emblem Warriors, the (2017) Minecraft: New Nintendo 3DS Edition – all of which only run on the (2011) Nintendo 3DS, the (2012) 3DS XL, the (2014) New Nintendo 3DS or the (2015) New Nintendo 3DS XL. And those four Nintendo, dual screen console, handheld models' most prominent feature was their ability to display stereoscopic 3D effects, aka, adding binocular depth information for binocular perception of 3D depth using a parallax barrier with a resolution of 400x240 pixels per eye and without the use of 3D glasses or additional accessories, with a six-axis motion sensor, which includes a 3-axis accelerometer and a 3-axis gyroscope; but only the last two models featured a second, analog "C" stick input on the right hand side of the device (good only for occasional functions such as camera control and aiming in third-person games), ZL/ZR controls, an improved camera, and other changes, allowing for functionality equivalent to the Circle Pad Pro add-on peripheral released for the previous models. The additional buttons were backwards-compatible with games programmed for use with Circle Pad Pro. But, in July 2019 the New 3D XL console production ceased and the product was removed from Nintendo's website. And Nintendo's 3DS family hardware was officially discontinued on Sept 16, 2022.

A second point of view from a single rendered image has an upper limit on how much parallax can be created and the surprise effect quickly wears off. The New 3DS used a ‘tracked 3D system’ where the viewing freedom was increased considerably by tracking the position of the user and adjusting the parallax barrier so that the left and right views are always directed to the user's eyes correctly, or to enlarge the stereoscopic sweet spot with multiple viewing zones thereby allowing multiple users to view the image at the same time, though they may also exhibit dead zones where only a non-stereoscopic or pseudoscopic image can be seen, if at all. Identification of the user's viewing angle was done by using a forward-facing camera above the display and image-processing software that would recognize the position of the user's face. Adjustment of the angle at which the left and right views were projected was done by electronically shifting the parallax barrier relative to the pixels. The crosstalk or percentage of light that deviates from one view to the other, at the best eye position might be 3%. The parallax barrier was behind the pixels and in front of the backlight which used 20-25% more backlight than it otherwise would.

However in 2010, the MIT Media Lab developed a double-layered LCD panel based approach called HR3D that would consume half as much power, doubling the battery life if used with devices like the Nintendo 3DS, without compromising screen brightness or resolution; other advantages include a larger viewing angle and maintaining the 3D effect when the screen is rotated. However, while capable of providing the perception of left–right movement parallax, no current display systems are known to simulate the perception of up–down movement parallax, so as objects increasingly distant from the plane of the display are presented, they may appear variously stretched or squashed to a viewer not positioned at the optimal distance from the display and displaying stereoscopic content without matching focal depth exhibits vergence-accommodation conflict.

Vergence or independent inward/outward rotation of eyes is engaged to fixate on objects and perceive them as single. Incorrect vergence response can cause double vision. Accommodation is the eye’s focusing mechanism and it is engaged to produce a sharp image on a retina. Both of these mechanisms are neurally linked forming the accommodation-convergence reflex of eyes. One can distinguish vergence distance – a distance of a point towards which both eyes are converging, and an accommodation distance – a distance of a region in space towards which the focus or refractive power of the crystalline lens has been adjusted to produce a sharp image on the retina. In normal conditions the human visual system expects vergence and accommodation distances to match. When viewing most artificial 3D images or displays, vergence and accommodation distances for the most part are mismatched, possibly causing a very unpleasant sensation for the viewer and visual fatigue and headaches after a short period of time and other virtual reality sickness [visually-induced perception of self-motion cause disorientation] symptoms such as general discomfort, eye strain, stomach awareness, nausea, vomiting, pallor, sweating, fatigue, drowsiness and apathy; perhaps due to the disparity in apparent motion between the visual and vestibular stimuli, that is, a disagreement between what the stimuli from the eyes and inner ear are sending to the brain.

Because the refresh rate is slower than what the brain processes, it causes a disconnect between the processing rate and the refresh rate, which causes the user to perceive glitches on the screen. When animations are poor, it causes another type of discord between what is expected and what is actually happening on the screen. When onscreen graphics do not keep the pace with the users' head movements, it can trigger a form of motion sickness.

Mismatched motion can be defined as a discrepancy between the motion of the simulation and the motion that the user expects. Generally, increasing the field of view increases incidence of simulator sickness symptoms. This relationship has been shown to be curvilinear, with symptoms approaching an asymptote for fields of view above 140°. Altering motion parallax distances to those less than the distance between the human eyes in large multiple-screen simulation setups can induce oculomotor distress, such as headaches, eyestrain, and blurred vision. There are fewer reports of oculomotor distress on smaller screens; however, most simulation setups with motion parallax effects can still induce eyestrain, fatigue, and general discomfort over time.

Viewing angle has been shown to increase a user's sickness symptoms, especially at extreme angles. One example of such an extreme angle would be when a user must look downwards a short distance in front of their virtual feet. As opposed to a forward viewing angle, an extreme downward angle such as this has been shown to markedly increase sickness in virtual environments. Time spent immersed in a virtual environment contributes to sickness symptom presence due to the increasing effects of fatigue on the user. Oculomotor symptoms are the most common to occur due to immersion time, but the nature of the user's movements (e.g., whole-body vs. head-only) is suggested to be the primary cause of nausea or physical sickness.

Certain gaming aspects are more likely to create issues, such as change in speed, walking up stairs, and jumping, which are all, unfortunately, fairly normal game functions in predominant genres.

Susceptibility to motion sickness is highest between the ages of 2 and 12. It then decreases rapidly until about age 21, and continues to decrease more slowly after that. It has been suggested that virtual reality sickness might follow a similar pattern, but more recent research has suggested that adults over the age of 50 are more susceptible than younger adults to virtual reality sickness.

Postural instability has been found to increase susceptibility to visually-induced motion sickness and with increased susceptibility to nausea and disorientation symptoms of virtual reality sickness. Because flicker in the display has been associated with increased risk of virtual reality sickness, people with a low threshold for detecting flicker may be more susceptible to virtual reality sickness.

Ethnicity: Asian people may be more susceptible to virtual reality sickness. Chinese women appear to be more susceptible to virtual reality sickness than European-American and African-American women; research suggests that they are more susceptible to vision-based motion sickness. Tibetans and Northeast Indians also appear to be more susceptible to motion sickness than Caucasian people, suggesting that they would also be more susceptible to virtual reality sickness, since susceptibility to motion sickness predicts susceptibility to a wide range of motion-sickness related disturbances.

Experience with the system: Users seem to become less likely to develop virtual reality sickness as they develop familiarity with a virtual reality system. Adaptation may occur as quickly as the second exposure to the virtual reality system.

Gender: Women are more susceptible than men to virtual reality sickness. This may be due to hormonal differences, it may be because women have a wider field of view than men, or gender differences in depth cue recognition. Women are most susceptible to virtual reality sickness during ovulation and a wider field of view is also associated with an increase in virtual reality sickness. In more recent research, there is some disagreement as to whether gender or sex is a clear factor in susceptibility to virtual reality sickness.

Health: Susceptibility to virtual reality sickness appears to increase in people who are not at their usual level of health, suggesting that virtual reality may not be appropriate for people who are in ill health. This includes people who are fatigued; have not had enough sleep; are nauseated; or have an upper respiratory illness, ear trouble, or influenza. Mental rotation ability: Better mental rotation ability appears to reduce susceptibility to virtual reality sickness, suggesting that training users in mental rotation may reduce the incidence of virtual reality sickness.

Field dependence / independence: Field dependence / independence is a measure of perceptual style. Those with strong field dependence exhibit a strong influence of surrounding environment on their perception of an object, whereas people with strong field independence show a smaller influence of surrounding environment on their perception of the object. While the relationship between field dependence/independence and virtual reality sickness is complex, it appears that, in general, people without a strong tendency towards one extreme or the other are most susceptible to virtual reality sickness. Motion sickness sensitivity: Those who are more sensitive to motion sickness in reality are also more sensitive to virtual reality sickness.

Stereoscopy is the production of the illusion of depth in a photograph, movie, or other two-dimensional image by the presentation of a slightly different image to each eye, which adds the first of these cues (stereopsis). The two images are then combined in the brain to give the perception of depth. Because all points in the image produced by stereoscopy focus at the same plane regardless of their depth in the original scene, the second cue, focus, is not duplicated and therefore the illusion of depth is incomplete. There are also mainly two effects of stereoscopy that are unnatural for human vision: (1) the mismatch between convergence and accommodation, caused by the difference between an object's perceived position in front of or behind the display or screen and the real origin of that light; and (2) possible crosstalk between the eyes, caused by imperfect image separation in some methods of stereoscopy.

Anatomically, there are 3 levels of binocular vision required to view stereo images:

- Simultaneous perception

- Fusion (binocular 'single' vision)

- Stereopsis

These functions develop in early childhood. Some people who have strabismus disrupt the development of stereopsis, however orthoptics treatment can be used to improve binocular vision. A person's stereoacuity determines the minimum image disparity they can perceive as depth. It is believed that approximately 12% of people are unable to properly see 3D images, due to a variety of medical conditions. According to another experiment up to 30% of people have very weak stereoscopic vision preventing them from depth perception based on stereo disparity. This nullifies or greatly decreases immersion effects of stereo to them.

The parallel viewing method uses an image pair with the left-eye image on the left and the right-eye image on the right. The fused three-dimensional image appears larger and more distant than the two actual images, making it possible to convincingly simulate a life-size scene. The viewer attempts to look through the images with the eyes substantially parallel, as if looking at the actual scene. This can be difficult with normal vision because eye focus and binocular convergence are habitually coordinated. One approach to decoupling the two functions is to view the image pair extremely close up with completely relaxed eyes, making no attempt to focus clearly but simply achieving comfortable stereoscopic fusion of the two blurry images by the "look-through" approach, and only then exerting the effort to focus them more clearly, increasing the viewing distance as necessary. Regardless of the approach used or the image medium, for comfortable viewing and stereoscopic accuracy the size and spacing of the images should be such that the corresponding points of very distant objects in the scene are separated by the same distance as the viewer's eyes, but not more; the average interocular distance is about 63 mm. Viewing much more widely separated images is possible, but because the eyes never diverge in normal use it usually requires some previous training and tends to cause eye strain.

Some stereoscopes are designed for viewing transparent photographs on film or glass, known as transparencies or diapositives and commonly called slides. The best-known formats for commercially issued stereo views on film are Tru-Vue, introduced in 1931, and View-Master, introduced in 1939 and still in production.

Head-mounted or wearable glasses may be used to view a see-through image imposed upon the real-world view, creating what is called augmented reality. This is done by reflecting the video images through partially reflective mirrors. The real-world view is seen through the mirrors' reflective surface. Experimental systems have been used for gaming, where virtual opponents may peek from real windows as a player moves about. This type of system is expected to have wide application in the maintenance of complex systems, as it can give a technician what is effectively "x-ray vision" by combining computer graphics rendering of hidden elements with the technician's natural vision. Additionally, technical data and schematic diagrams may be delivered to this same equipment, eliminating the need to obtain and carry bulky paper documents.

Augmented stereoscopic vision is also expected to have applications in surgery, as it allows the combination of radiographic data (CAT scans and MRI imaging) with the surgeon's vision.

There are two categories of 3D viewer technology, the passive viewers filter constant streams of binocular input to the appropriate eye. On most passive displays every other row of pixels is polarized for one eye or the other. This method is also known as being interlaced. The viewer wears low-cost eyeglasses which also contain a pair of opposite polarizing filters. As each filter only passes light which is similarly polarized and blocks the opposite polarized light, each eye only sees one of the images, and the effect is achieved.

Notice that when the Left Joy-Con is configured for horizontal use as mini-controller, then each of the Advanced 8 buttons on it is also configured to play exactly as its corresponding Basic 8 button on the Right mini-controller. And that means, for most 1st party games, all basic game control can be mastered by using the Basic 8 buttons as labeled on the Right mini-controller.

For reference purposes, the Basic 8 can be stated using either using just the Right Joy-Con button name, or for Players using a Left Joy-Con, can be combined with a slash, like "A / ▸ Right" to denote that if your single Left Joy-Con used horizontally does not have a button labeled A, then find the button "labeled" ▸ Right (that is, the one that has a concave, hollowed out, recessed triangle icon that is pointing to the right), and it will function the same. So, for any multiplayer modes of the 3 Mario games Super Mario, Kart and Odyssey, all playable character control is around using the Basic 8 buttons. Note also that if one becomes accustomed to playing with a Right mini-controller for horizontal use, then it will take a few minutes of usage to reprogram your fingers to use a Left mini-controller configured for horizonal use because the exact positions of the all the Basic 8 play buttons changes, but only slightly (and vice versa).

The Basic 8 can also be thought of as the Basic 7 to control your Player character, because the + / - button has limited, less frequent usage when playing Joy-Con mini-controller -supported games including our Mario games (like just pausing the game and or for accessing menus). Other than the + / - button, there remain four Face buttons: X / ▴ Up; A / ▸ Right; B / ▾ Down; Y / ◂ Left; and then three more: a Right Stick / Left Stick analog (degree of tilt makes a difference just like a gas pedal on a vehicle) control (thumb or joy) stick; and two shoulder buttons: a R / L shoulder Bumper button and a ZR / ZL back-behind shoulder Trigger button (— Z being a third [3D, depth] dimension after X [width] and Y [height] for 3D graphics — all advanced concepts and skills [like the Stick, Bumper, and Trigger] for young and inexperienced gamers)

4 Face Buttons (X / ▴ Up; A / ▸ Right; B / ▾ Down; Y / ◂ Left)

Notice, firstly, that the four Face buttons on a left Joy-Con used horizontally could, in one sense, duplicate but "simplify" (for the young and inexperienced) the directional d-pad's tilting mechanics.

Secondly, the face buttons’ (d-pad-like) direction will be relative to how the Joy-Con mini-controller is held.

Typically the left and right Joy-Cons rest in your left and right hands, letting you access the analog sticks and face buttons easily with your thumbs. You can also turn a Joy-Con sideways with the attachment rail facing away from you and use it as a simpler controller. This enables two-player gaming out of the box without needing to buy more Joy-Cons. The asymmetrical design of the Joy-Cons become apparent in this configuration, because the left features the analog stick on the far left side and the face buttons in the middle, while the right features the face buttons on the far right side and the analog stick in the middle. Whether the Joy-Cons are awkward to use in this position is a matter of hand size and personal taste—I didn't mind either after a few moments to get used to the different spacing of the controls. source: https://www.pcmag.com/reviews/nintendo-switch

Nintendo has had a long history in the video game market. What started out as a toy company soon became the number one name in the home console market. Over time, Nintendo has produced multiple consoles, and while its competitors often seem to make only minor adjustments to their own controller designs, Nintendo has taken a more unique approach.

Nintendo has a habit of scrapping its designs completely, carrying over only a few design concepts between console and controller iterations. While it may frustrate some fans who have a particular favorite, it does make the evolution of the company's controllers pretty interesting.

While Nintendo's first console was technically the Japan-exclusive Color-TV Game, its controllers were built in to the system itself, and are therefore not often considered Nintendo's true first controller. Instead, the Nintendo Entertainment System (or the Famicom in Japan) is widely considered to be the first Nintendo home console with controllers.

The NES' controllers are iconically stiff and awkward, appearing as an oblong-shaped brick. The design of this controller is simple, but genius, with only a few buttons appearing overall, allowing for great accessibility from gamers of all ages and skill levels.

The controller has two "face" buttons, labelled "A" and "B", appearing in that iconic red color, and the controller features one of the first instances of a "D-Pad" (the 'D' standing for 'Directional'.) Originally designed by Gunpei Yokoi for the Game and Watch series of handhelds, the "Cross-Pad" made its way to home consoles here.

A 1990 Super NES (Nintendo Entertainment System) controller – the "Family Computer" aka Famicom version is Nintendo's home country brand.

After the 8-bit mini-console became a smash hit, Nintendo released its 16-bit successor. The Super NES Classic has fewer games than the NES Classic, but the jump in console generations means you can play some of the best 16-bit video games of all time.

If you didn't play the games when they first came out or haven't tried them through other ways, the SNES Classic is a must-have for gaming historians. Some of the best games ever made are here, and that's not hyperbole. Good luck finding one at its original price, though. This is an expensive system for collectors.
