It refers to something we have little to no control over. It also refers to something that potentially can be the source of defensive acts, a source of personal and interpersonal confusion.

Possession as experience

How to circumscribe feeling experience? How to capture subjectivity and other “what it is like” experiences of possession that presumably we share with other animals? What is the affectivity and emotional life that cuts across species at some basic implicit levels?

A machine does not experience possession. It does not possess. It might be programmed to say “mine!” when detecting something in the environment but that does not qualify it as experiencing possession. We might consider “Siri,” the virtual interlocutor of my smartphone, to be an actual person. But that is just a figment of our imagination, our irresistible tendency to project mental attributes into inanimate things and other simulacrums. When talking to Siri and listening to “her” answers, we are interacting with a host of Apple Inc. engineers who came up with this smart feature mimicking reality. Siri is a programmed avatar, not a person. Our proclivity to project mental attributes into physical things and artifacts should not be simply derided as in the common spoofing of our inclinations toward superstitions and other “pseudo-” and “pre-”scientific claims. Those are indeed revealing of who we are psychologically and probably what makes us unique in the animal kingdom: imaginative and fantasy prone creatures inclined to impute intentions and complex mental states to physical, inanimate things. I will have more opportunities to come back to the particularly unique human propensity toward animism and the projection of intelligent life into material things (i.e., see Chapter 4).1 This propensity is central to the psychology of possession, the necessary ingredient for most of our irresistible attachment to things.

Machines sense but don’t feel. We, like other animals, do feel the world around us; we do not just sense it as a thermostat would. Most animals, including us, are much more than thermostats. A thermostat senses temperature changes, serving the specific function of controlling and regulating the ambient air of a contained environment. Thermostats, as “autonomous” feedback loop systems, do control the atmosphere but they do not feel it in the way we feel warm or cold. Self-regulation happens at a very different level, a subjective level that defines psychology as a distinct field, in contrast to the deterministic fields of physics and engineering in particular. This explains why there is a world of engineers and a world of psychologists, two professions that should not be confounded. Both professions have their own specific, ontologically different objects. Some grey areas exist of course (e.g., machine–user interaction) but machines are not people, because they do not feel and have no emotions. They do not have feelings, but are just astute detectors that sense with no meanings attached to it.

Feeling experience entails mental states, sensing does not. For example, we do not “sense” pain, but we feel it. Pain is an experience referring to a particular mental state that we recognize and eventually can describe to ourselves or someone else, or simply refer to via specific emotional expressions. The expression of pain makes its corresponding mental state public, hence readable and shareable with other “feeling” creatures who can relate, resonate, sympathize, maybe even empathize with it.

Fundamentally, most animals are feeling creatures, communicating with each other in reference to mental states: happiness, contentment, arousal, pain, sadness, disgust, eagerness. The world of feeling creatures is colored by affective values that pull and push. It is a “hot” and emotionally colorful world that is much more than the cold world of machines, however complex those machines might be, and however closely they might simulate the colorful world of feeling experience. They are just approximations of the real thing. 2

The point I am trying to drive home here is that possession is primarily a feeling experience, like pain. It refers to complex mental states that are the foundation of the psychology of possession. Like pain, joy, or sadness, possession is felt and not merely sensed by those creatures endowed with feeling experience and the accompanying “what it is like” phenomenal or P-awareness. The question, however, is how feeling experience and its accompanying awareness compares across ages and species, as well as across levels of psychological complexity and depth. One way to address this question is to consider first what might be the criteria for endowing a creature with “feeling” as opposed to just machine-like sensing experiences.

Criteria for minimal feeling experience (as opposed to mere sensing)

It is common to link feeling experience to higher-order cognitive processes associated with late-developing cortical structures. From this perspective, one should not attribute any kind of feeling awareness but rather just sensing, machine-like awareness to creatures that are not, or not yet, endowed with higher cortical structures, namely a mammalian forebrain. But this view is challenged by empirical evidence of goal-directed, purposive behaviors in decorticated animals and anencephalic children (children born without cortex).3 In general, it appears that feeling experience does not have to be explicit and mediated by higher symbolic processes like language. Infants as well as most animals could be endowed with the potential for feeling awareness, depending on what criteria are used.

In his argument in support of a consciousness without cortex, Merker proposes that in “the most basic and general sense” what qualifies for consciousness (here by extension the putative awareness and the feeling experience of possession) is “the state or condition presupposed by any experience whatsoever” (p. 63). This would mean that only “experiencing” creatures could possess as construed here: those who are capable of having subjective “what it is like” experiences. This proposal, however, begs the question of what qualifies as having “any feeling experience whatsoever.” In particular, what is having feeling experience and awareness versus not having any of it or just machine-like sensing experience?

I propose that to have feeling experience is to have an affective life that is made of perceived values (or qualities) such as pain, pleasure, or cravings. Having experience, hence having an affective life, should transcend the mere recording of raw sensations as “signals” by an organism functioning like a thermostat. Inversely, not having experience is to sense the world by simply recording raw sensory signals that trigger automatic, predictable responses as in the output behavior of computers or thermostats. Again, these automata sense but do not feel. One entails minimal subjective experience (feelings), not the other, even though output behavior might be homologous for third party observers (e.g., fleeing of a cockroach versus the fleeing of a foot soldier under attack).

Feelings as opposed to raw sensory signals are expressed in emotions via particular bodily movements (e.g., facial expression, or a particular dynamic of motion or signaling as in screaming). As already mentioned, it is the affective life revealed in expressive emotions that distinguishes sentient creatures from mere machines and automata. The former feel and are potentially conscious, the latter are not. Feeling experience adds values to an organism’s encounter with the world. More importantly, in relation to possession, it gives purpose and orientation to actions performed by that organism (e.g., defending, protecting, acquiring, controlling).

This is the constitutive element of any form of what we refer to as consciousness (the state or condition presupposed by feeling experience), and by extension the necessary prerequisite of a minimal possession awareness that can be imputed to most animals and very young infants.

In short, affectivity and emotions guide actions and elevate behaviors above the register of mere automatic and mechanistic responses. Automata respond; they do not act proper. Contrary to sentient (feeling) organisms, they respond like thermostats do in relation to temperature fluctuations within a pre-set, calibrated range. Thermostats do not act to avoid hot or cold, nor are they oriented toward a gain of comfort (pleasure or the maintenance of good feelings). Machines do have, however, the superior power to find and apply algorithms to resolve complex problems with reliable success (see the chess match between the IBM Deep Blue machine and Garry Kasparov). Machines can, in some cold sense, think and resolve problems, but they can’t feel and for this reason have no potential for possession, except perhaps in science fictions (e.g., the computer HAL 9000 experiencing “fear” in Clarke and Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey).

The necessary qualifier for having minimal possession awareness is, accordingly, the feeling experience that elevates organisms from mere responders to volitional actors (goal-oriented and purposeful beings in a world made of affective values: pleasures, pains, envies). Possession awareness must co-emerge with feeling experience, both mutually necessary and co-defining.

Possession is therefore affective and emotional in origin, rather than cognitive in the etymological sense of consciousness (con-scientia or “with-knowledge”). If possession has anything to do with knowledge or cognition, it is with “hot” not cold cognition: what feels good or bad, what is pleasurable or not, ultimately what feels right and what feels wrong.

Children in their development, as I will try to show, demonstrate that the explicit conscious “content” of possession (explicit and conceptual awareness of ownership, entitlement, and ultimately property rights) rests upon and is eventually added to this basic pre-reflective and implicit affective process that distinguishes us from machines. But this implies major steps in brain and behavior development.

Within this theoretical framework, the question is: when can we say that an organism has feeling experiences, hence fills the criteria for having minimal feeling of possession? Do cockroaches feel? Are cold blooded species (fish, octopus, reptiles) and those which have not evolved a mammalian brain precluded from having possession experience? Do birds feel? What about human fetuses or young infants? When do we start to feel, and hence have the potential to have minimal experience of possession?

Looking at the brain, isolating neural networks and brain structures that are predictably associated in time with feeling experiences can help in determining whether an organism “feels” something and might be endowed with subjective experience, therefore qualifying for potential possession experience. Inversely, just looking at behavior and emotional expressions that are predictably associated with feeling experiences (e.g., pain) can do the same. But first, “peripheral” receptor systems (e.g., pain, auditory, vestibular, light, olfactory, or gustatory sensitivity) have to be functional and connected (projecting) to some higher centers of the nervous system for further processing and motor/vegetative responses.

Implicit versus explicit feeling experience

The feeling experience of pain in a fetus may be comparable to my experience of pain as it refers to an overall negative state (i.e., a state that puts the organism on sympathetic stress alert to be avoided and cancelled out as soon as possible). However, my own and a fetus’s pain threshold are most probably not comparable, our subjective experience of pain quite different. Let’s say that I get a finger caught in a slamming door. Aside from screaming, I would eventually look for a culprit, blame myself, search for sympathy by publicly feeling sorry for myself. My direct experience of feeling pain, the one I might share with a fetus, is quickly transformed and re-described via language and other higher self-conscious thought processes. From an implicit, direct experience, it becomes explicit and socially situated.

In the same way that it is important to distinguish implicit and explicit levels of pain experience, it is also important to distinguish between the implicit and explicit levels of feeling possession. This will be particularly relevant when discussing the psychology of possession from the perspective of development (Part II of the book).

As we shall see, the development of possession parallels the development of self and social (people) understanding. It fundamentally transits from a world of experience that is embodied and implicit to a world of experience that, in addition to being embodied and implicit, is also embodied and conscientiously shared with others via symbolic and cultural devices like language.

Implicit and explicit feeling experiences are ontologically different and emerge at different points in time during development, one preceding the other without strictly replacing the other. Implicit experience continues to play a central role in our adult conscious life. But in development, both come to co-exist and interact in complex ways. In other words, in psychological development, the child adds “layers” or levels of feeling experience, progressively adding layers of explicitness to primordial and deeply rooted implicit layers of awareness. There comes a point in development when both implicit and explicit awareness co-exist and interact in complex ways, our conscious mind transiting and voyaging through these layers of awareness. This may all sound very speculative but in fact there are numerous and increasing numbers of empirical studies that point to such co-existing levels of awareness: implicit and explicit levels of memory, concepts, thoughts, decision making processes, and social preference. These co-existing and interacting levels of awareness across the various domains emerge early in development, and certainly by the middle of second year, if not earlier. It is well established, for example, that implicit procedural memory exists in infancy, long before the child can explicitly reminisce about events and ways of resolving problems.4 Some research even shows that 18-month-old children, surreptitiously presented with two dolls hugging one another, are subliminally primed to help an adult who has accidently dropped something on the floor!5 This remarkable finding demonstrates that various layers of mental processing (i.e., implicit and explicit experience) co-exist and interact very early in life, at least by the time children learn to speak, and possibly even earlier. 6

Origins of feeling experience

A rich body of neuroanatomical as well as behavioral evidence points to the fact that it is reasonable to think that implicit feeling awareness, hence subjective experience, is already present at birth, possibly even in the womb. This is a rather revolutionary idea considering that, not so long ago, the idea of feeling-less infants (i.e., nonverbal children) was the default assumption.

Until fairly recently, the Zeitgeist was to deny infants any form of worthwhile feeling experience (phenomenal awareness). Proof of this is that in the 1940s and 1950s, surgery without anesthesia was routinely performed on infants and young children. Modern surgeons conveniently paralyzed squirming infants by injection of curare or similar paralytic agents. Under such circumstances, adults recalled excruciating pain during surgery. But patients were not believed and the practice went on for twenty years. As pointed out by Dennett: “The fact that most of the patients were infants and small children may explain this credibility gap.”7 Even today, local anesthetics are not routine in painful procedures on newborns such as heel prick and circumcision, even by pediatricians practicing in state of the art maternity hospitals. The Zeitgeist continues to be that infants have either no feelings or few feelings, or that feeling experience at this early stage may not be of any consequence because it is not remembered (infantile amnesia). Such a rationale raises questions when looking at the brain as well as behavior in prenatal and postnatal development.

Looking at brain development during the prenatal and postnatal period suggests that the necessary neurological prerequisites for feeling experience may already be in place by 8 weeks after conception, meaning when the sperm met the egg! Here in a nutshell is what we know today about the emergence of the brain and neural growth from conception to birth. This emergence is astonishing in its pace and complexity, considering that the brain is probably the most complex system in the universe. It reminds us of the great biological forces behind development. It takes only 4 weeks from conception for the neural tube to be formed from layers of cells on the embryonic disc.8 Only one extra week is needed for the basic five-part structure of the brain to be anatomically differentiated and clearly visible (i.e., telecephalon and diencephalon of the forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain, and the spinal cord). By 11 weeks of gestation (not 3 months after conception!), medulla, cerebellum, inferior and superior colliculus, as well as both cerebral hemispheres covering the diencephalon are also clearly visible. 9

From then on and for a few years, both hemispheres grow in surface areas via folding grooves and convolutions. This growth reflects rapid and exponential connection networks among synapses as well as myelination of axons providing insulation (fatty “white matter”) for better transmission of electrochemical nerve impulses. By 2 years of age, the child’s brain already weighs 80 percent of its lifetime maximum weight.10 Let’s now look more closely at what we know about development at a more microscopic level: the level of the brain’s building blocks, the neurons.

In terms of neural growth, between 10 and 26 weeks’ gestational age, neurons are produced at a rate of 250,000 a minute, leading to overproduction. Beyond 26 weeks, more than half of the produced nerve cells are selectively pruned and die. The surviving 100 billion will eventually form the adult brain. 11 All of this development is indeed humbling. We should always keep it in the back of our mind when thinking about what it means to be present, alive, and having experience in this world.

Regarding connection between cells, there is also an overproduction of synapses that continues beyond birth, with peaking periods that vary across brain regions. 12 Synaptogenesis continuing after birth is not homogeneous and synchronous across brain regions. For example, post-mortem data indicate that synaptic density peaks earlier in the auditory cortex (3 months) compared to the middle frontal gyrus (15 months). 13 This kind of growth asynchrony is reflected, for example, in the sequential development of sense modalities in the womb and beyond (i.e., vision lag).

In short, these facts remind us that brain emergence, and the neural (sensory) machinery that necessarily underlies implicit feeling experience, is fast, remarkably precise, and predictable in its unfolding. To the naked eye or through the lens of a microscope, it is an explosive and amazingly well-programmed growth. In relation to putative first feeling experience, brain development puts in place within 8 weeks the potential for fetuses to sense the world, hence also the necessary prerequisite to eventually feel it: the potential for first minimal, obviously implicit, and very rudimentary feeling experience. Let us not forget, however, that feeling experience rests on the prerequisite of an ability to sense the world, as machines do. What I have tried to show is that, in humans, such necessary sensory “machinery” matures within weeks of conception and long before birth. In its development and within the confines of the maternal womb, fetal research shows that this actually recapitulates the emergence order of the main sensory systems in the course of species evolution. The sensory machinery (sense modalities) of fetuses matures in the same sequential order as our ancestral species.14 Somesthetic sensitivity (skin and body feelings) matures first. This sensitivity corresponds to tactile (skin pressure), vestibular (posture and balance), and pain stimulation (tissue damage). It is followed by the maturation of chemosensory sensitivity that combines olfaction and gustation (i.e., smell and taste), followed by audition (pitch, amplitude, and phrasing of sounds), and finally by vision (light and optic array). From this, we can conclude that the necessary sensory prerequisites of first feeling experience are in place at least by the third semester of gestation. But when can we say that first feeling experiences actually emerge in development? We shall see in more detail in the second part of the book, on the developmental origins of possession, that new ways of observing fetuses (three- and four-dimensional sonic echography and image scanning) suggest that already by the last trimester fetuses express emotions such as “happiness” via smiling and “sadness” via frowning of the eyebrows and lowering of the corners of the lips in the same way newborns express such mental states at birth and beyond. 15 More intriguing is the fact that nociceptive (pain) receptors appear first in and around the mouth area at around 7 weeks after conception. They rapidly extend to the palmar surface of the hands by 11 weeks, and the rest of the skin and mucosal surfaces by 20 weeks. 16

In all, this suggests that in trying to find the roots of “feeling” experience, including possession, above and beyond sensing, we should probably already look in the womb for its embryonic stage.

On possessing oneself: implicit self-evidence

At some basic level, feeling experience carries with it a fundamental self-evidence property. It is that my feeling experiences of the world are mine, and can only be mine and nobody else’s. This is true no matter what, and to the extent that I don’t take drugs or show symptoms of schizophrenic autism or any other kind of psychosis. As phenomenological philosophers in the European tradition of Husserl, Merleau-Ponty, Sartre, and many others, but more recently Dan Zahavi or Shaun Gallagher, would claim, this self-evidence comes for free with any kind of feeling experience. 17 It is an implicit given. In the same way, James Gibson18 in his ecological approach to perception proposes that perceiving the world always necessarily entails co-perceiving oneself as perceiver and actor in the world. One implies the other, no matter what, like the two sides of the same coin. This is a simple, yet powerful intuition that is theoretically helpful, accounting for much of what we see in the development of children and in devastating instances of psychopathology like schizophrenia. For these empirical reasons, there is good reason to endorse such implicit “self-evidence” that feeling would necessarily entail.19 However, before presenting this empirical ground for siding with the phenomenologists, one should acknowledge other philosophical and psychological perspectives adopting radically different epistemological starting points. These views are that the mine-ness of experience is most likely an illusion and a cognitive reconstruction rather than a necessary given.20 Accordingly, self-perception would be more the product of an inference and a mental representation rather than an implicit “direct” counterpart of any acts of direct perception as suggested by Gibson. 21

I would say simply that cognitive reconstruction views are untenable when considering very young infants, as well as adults suffering mental and other self disorders found particularly in schizophrenia but also in other psychotic symptoms.

Our own observations of young infants, together with many others that I will have the chance to review in more details in Part II of the book, point to the fact that we are born with the basic intuition of what belongs to our own feeling experience and what is not. Infants a few hours old show unambiguous discrimination between self and non-self touch. We were able to demonstrate that newborns root significantly more in the direction of another person’s finger that touches one of their cheeks compared to when one of their own fingers comes spontaneously in contact with the same cheek. They discriminate between self-produced “double-touch” of simultaneous cheek and finger touching and the “single” touch of a non-self finger.22 This simple observation tells us, among other empirical evidence found in neonates, that we are born with the potential for the implicit sense of exclusive mine-ness of experience, something that is probably the necessary phenomenal prerequisite of psychological development, its necessary subjective seed. That my feelings are mine is self-evident and does not have to be an indirect representational reconstruction. If that were the case, it is doubtful that neonates would show discrimination between double and single touch experience. Our observations imply that there is from birth the potential self-evidence property of feeling experience.

On being possessed

A look at the anomalous experience of psychotic adults who suffer from great cognitive disorganization and uncontrollable hallucinations within the schizophrenia spectrum demonstrates how fundamental and actually basic self-evident mine-ness experience is, the sine qua non condition of our sanity. It shows clearly that self-evident mine-ness of feeling experience is the cornerstone of the ways we create meanings and bring coherence to our experience of being alive in this world: something that is ineffable (hard to put words on) and pre-reflective (implicit) by nature.

Loss of self-evident mine-ness of experience can be pathological and long lasting, just as it can be temporary and provoked by drugs and trance-inducing rituals that are so pervasive across religions and cultures. Speaking tongues and other possessed states are symptomatic of self-evident feeling experience transmuted (mentally delegated) to a fictive entity that intrudes individual consciousness, be it the devil or a dead ancestor. Trance states can transform the implicit self-evidence typically accompanying feeling experience into the embodied allo-evidence of another. Possessed individuals are literally invaded and under the spell of another. There is experiential loss of self-control, until the individual snaps out of the trance state. Aside from religious rituals, hypnosis is a good, more secular example of a trance-like state. It continues to be successfully exploited in psychotherapy and psychoanalysis, in the footsteps of Charcot (1825–93) in his pioneer research on hysteria and other neurotic symptoms shown to be of psychological origin, as well as Freud in his early practice of psychoanalysis (c. 1895). 23 Such induced temporary disturbance and loss of subjectivity is similar in some fundamental ways to chronic psychosis like schizophrenia.

Refined examination of the subjective, first person perspective accounts of hundreds of schizophrenic individuals reveals that, first and foremost, schizophrenia and allied symptoms are disorders of minimal self-experience, including at its core the self-evident mine-ness experience.24 It is typical for individuals suffering the atrocious ills of schizophrenia to report that although they rationally, thus explicitly, know that their thoughts originate from within them and are not hallucinations proper, these thoughts are nonetheless not felt as generated by them. There is no implicit sense of self-agency in thinking or generating thoughts, and they are thus somehow “possessed” rather than in possession as discussed above. It is a loss of thought “ipseity” (from the Latin word ipse, self), in other words the loss of the mine-ness of thinking one’s own thoughts. Losing this basic and implicit sense of self is devastating, of almost unimaginable horror, as probably best conveyed by Elyn Saks’s vivid, very personal, and detailed account of her own journey into schizophrenia: 25

This experience is much harder, and weirder, to describe than extreme fear or terror. Most people know what it is like to be seriously afraid. If they haven’t felt it themselves, they’ve at least seen a movie, or read a book, or talked to a frightened friend – they can at least imagine it. But explaining what I’ve come to call “disorganization” is a different challenge altogether. Consciousness gradually loses its coherence. One’s center gives way. The center cannot hold. The “me” becomes a haze, and the solid center from which one experiences reality breaks up like a bad radio signal. There is no longer a sturdy vantage point from which to look out, take things in, assess what’s happening. No core holds things together, providing the lens through which to see the world, to make judgments and comprehend risk. Random moments of time follow one another. Sights, sounds, thoughts, and feelings don’t go together. No organizing principle takes successive moments in time and puts them together in a coherent way from which sense can be made. And it’s all taking place in slow motion. Delusions and hallucinations are an intrinsic part of the diagnosis of schizophrenia and its self-disorganization, including voices as running commentaries on the person’s behavior or thoughts, some sort of inescapable hyper-reflectivity but from a third party perspective that invades the individual who has lost basic self-evidence and an implicit trust that subjective experience belongs to oneself, a feeling experience that is not self-specifying anymore but rather diffused and confused with a world that is chaotic: the forceful, uncontrollable voices and intrusive thoughts that have no overarching narrative structure, no meaningful organization.

Such psychopathologies point to the fact that to function and experience the world normally, self-evidence and the basic feeling experience that one’s thoughts and perceptions belong to oneself is a necessity. It is indispensable, an absolute pre-requisite to avoid mental invasion and the loss of minimal self-reference. How easy it is for us to take for granted the fact that these gestures, this voice, this vision belong to no one else and no other source than me. Without this basic self-evident feeling experience, we are at a loss. Losing it is indeed devastating. We shall also see that this is the primordial prerequisite of psychological development that starts in the womb.

The me and the mine

William James, in his seminal discussion of the self as psychological construct states: “A man’s Self is the sum total of all that he can call his, not only his body and his psychic powers, but his clothes and his house, his wife and children, his ancestors and friends, his reputation and works, his lands, and yacht and bank-account. All these things give him the same emotions. If they wax and prosper, he feels triumphant; if they dwindle and die away, he feels cast down.” 26

The question is, how do we come up with a “me” concept that includes a great number of things existing outside of our physical envelope, and therefore that are physically non-self entities, literally incorporated as parts of our bodily selves? The process of incorporation, when you think of it, is a rather curious propensity of ours. The question is even more salient and puzzling in light of William James’s further consideration: “it is clear that between what a man calls me and what he simply calls mine the line is difficult to draw. We feel and act about certain things that are ours very much as we feel and act about ourselves” (p. 291). Here, James points to the fact that the differentiation between self and objects can become blurry and eventually disappear with certain objects that are assimilated to the self via the elusive process of incorporation. By this process, some objects become part of the “embodied” self, an intrinsic part of the entity that feels and acts, the entity we perceive and conceptually identify as “me.”

If we take this observation seriously, we can contemplate the depth of its psychological meaning. It is profound because mental sanity rests on the basic sense of where we stand in relation to things. Again, the mental suffering associated with psychotic bouts such as schizophrenia comes primarily from a blurring of the experience of what corresponds to the self and what corresponds to outside things. So, for example, in the midst of a crisis, a psychotic might hear voices in his head that he wrongly attributes as originating from outside his body, or he might perceive self-motion (own movements) as allo-motion (external, non-self movements). As we have seen, this is a source of great cognitive confusion associated with excruciating anxieties, and dramatic affective and existential consequences for the individual.

At both implicit and explicit levels of experience, the psychology of possession rests on a primordial process of incorporation to the embodied self: a literal process of projection and identification that leads to some assimilative re-embodiment of things to the self. It is a process of absorption and digestion into the embodied self, and eventually retention and expulsion as described by Freud27 in his pleasure-related control experience of the anal stage in psychosexual development (i.e., pleasure of the sphincter as primary erogenous zone).

This primordial process of incorporation in the literal and etymological sense of the word refers to the combining of substances, the absorption into the corpus (Latin word for body) of something that is foreign to it. This process leads to the often illusory, but self-evident feeling that it is “mine.” It is from incorporation that arises the feeling of “mine-ness” projected onto physical objects (my car, my toothbrush, my chair) or persons (my girlfriend, my mother, my husband, my teacher). It arises from the process by which things, objectified as external to us (a book, a glass, an individual), but also possibly things that we feel emanating from within us (a novel idea, a concept, the solution to a problem, a style, a gesture), become also experienced as ours and nobody else’s. It is the bottom-line process of all propensities toward creating an exclusive world that enlarges the self with things possessed (i.e., belongings). As stated by William James, we do project and identify with things that become an intrinsic part of us and who we are for ourselves as well as the outside world. It is the process by which objects are somehow transmuted into belongings that become patently ours through our eyes but also the eyes of others.

Incorporation to the self is not limited to surrounding material entities. As everyone knows, especially divorce and other patent lawyers, it also applies to practices, styles, ideas, and manners, even people (my wife, my child, my maid, my priest). In fact the process of incorporation is what underlies all of our certainties about what belongs to us, and what we feel we are entitled to. Interestingly, at the group level, it is an analogous process by which laws induct companies, literally incorporating responsibilities and entitlements into institutions that become moral persons (Inc.).

Behind such incorporation to the self, there are two basic propensities emerging in development, especially exacerbated in humans, commonly referred to as projection and identification. The feeling experience of possession entails the complex processes of projection and identification, particularly when such experience becomes explicit and objectified, when the child grabs an object and claims to the world: “That’s mine!” (see next chapter). Projection is a two-way, mutual assimilation of self and object. When claiming “That’s mine!” the child in his words claims assimilation of the object to the embodied self, but also the reverse: the expulsion of self into the object, a dual phenomenon that Freud and followers like Ferenczi label respectively “exterojection” and “introjection” of the self to the object.

Freud in his writing insists that this dual process is characteristic of normal psychological functioning from the outset, and not just symptomatic of his patients’ psychopathology. Rightly, Freud extrapolates the crucial contrast experience of what is inside and outside of the body afforded by the natural, instinctive inclination of infants to ingest and reject food. 28 Freud probably did not know at the time that this inclination is expressed already in utero.

It is now well documented that, by the last trimester of gestation, fetuses engage in much sucking and ingestion, as well as dejection of surrounding amniotic fluid. The potential of an implicit contrast experience of what is inside and outside of the body is therefore present very early on and is probably where the feeling of possession finds its budding, embryonic roots. But obviously, things develop and change radically. Their meanings change, from infancy and throughout the lifespan. The dual process of introjection and exterojection, the experience of ingestion and rejection, inside versus outside of body, the implicit as well as explicit experience of things possessed, find different meanings in the history of individuals. Our relation to food changes with age as much as our relation to things and people. This relation is also context dependent. In Samoa being fat and big is associated with power and being served by others, not having to budge much in daily chores. In the industrial Western world, the USA in particular, it is associated with poverty. Some become health freaks, others compulsive junk eaters. Some become jealous individuals, others free spirits. Some try to get rid of superfluous things and others cultivate the hoarding of wealth and power. It all depends, but it all has in common the quest for a self-identity: trying to specify what is “me” in relation to others. In this common quest, what separates me from mine is elusive and forms the major grey area of self-psychology. This grey area extends from and separates embodied self and the world. It is the zone that is at the core of issues regarding the feeling of possession and the general process of incorporation. It is the grey area that arises from an intrinsic elusiveness in the determination of what individuates possessions that exist outside of the bodily envelope but are felt, and eventually objectified as being intrinsic parts of the embodied self: my house, my children, my car. It raises the fundamental question of what is the experiential demarcation between self and world. What determines the feeling of such demarcation and the point where me and mine are felt the same, thus experientially merging to become interchangeable like me and my face or my heart, but also my wife, my car, and my chair – at this point in time in this crowded restaurant: all felt as possessions of mine?

Are these shoes or these ideas mine? Yes, of course, but on what basis? Possession as self-experience is a grey area of psychology, dynamic and underspecified. The limits of entitlement and control over things, above and beyond our own subjective experience of entitlement, can only be socially negotiated.

Ooka Tadasuke was a Samurai turned judge during the eighteenth-century Edo period of Japanese history (1600–1838). He is legendary for his haiku type verdicts. Ooka Tadasuke’s verdicts are much more than sanctioning sentences. Like haiku poetry, they open gates to deep reflections on essential issues, one of them being the limits and determination of possession. Best known is the legendary verdict pronounced toward a hungry and poor student who had only bland rice to eat. The student would eat his bowl of rice sitting on the steps of a restaurant, augmenting his diet with the rich odors escaping from the kitchen. The cook caught the student, accusing him of stealing the smell of his cooking. The case was brought to Ooka Tadasuke, whose verdict was for the student to pay back the cook with the sound of money passed from hand to hand. This verdict points to the elusiveness of entitlement and value equivalence. Indeed, is the water of the stream running through my property mine? What about the style of a drawing copied and reproduced in a magazine? Can an idea, the invention of a color scheme, or a signature character still be “mine” once it is public and reproduced with slight alterations? Who owns the air inside my apartment? What are good enough reasons for screaming “Thief!” and how should victims of theft be compensated? What is subjective equivalence (i.e., the perceived interchangeable value of things that are ontologically distinct like apples and oranges)? These questions are not only economic and political. They are first and foremost revealing of the complex psychology of feeling possession.

In William James’s terms, the sense of possession is rooted in the conflation of the “me” and of the “mine.” Questions remain, however, as to what might drive this conflation, and ultimately what might be gained from it since such conflation renders the limits that separate self and world blurry. The answer lies, I think, in the fact that ultimately the process of appropriation underlying possession is about social power but also – paradoxically – about the promotion of belongingness: the experience of social affiliation and ultimately the promotion of social harmony.

Envy and jealousy

In absolute solitude and with no potential aggressors, there would be no reason to experience possession. At the most basic level, possession is an experience that is grounded in the fear of a threat: the threat of being “dispossessed.” It derives from and is the necessary counterpart of a fear of losing control over entities that are incorporated to the self, but also over one’s own life and integrity. The experience of possession is thus, across species, in essence defensive in relation to others, whether others are conspecifics or not. The fear of losing control is therefore inseparable from the feeling of possession.

Social competition that is the evolutionary context of possession determines particular perceptions of mental states (feelings) and their public expression (emotions).29 These are recognizable in the human affective spinoffs of possession that are envy and jealousy. If the drive and comfort of having control over things underlies possession, the loss of it determines and is a crucial and necessary counterpart of such experience. Indeed, aside from fear, it is when we actually lose control over an object of possession that we gauge the power of our attachment. Often, it is only when we lose something that we realize how much we cared for it, sometimes with devastating affective exaggeration as in the case of envy and jealousy.

Ancient Greek philosophers discussed envy as self-reproach, the reproach of not possessing what others have.30 In this sense, and interestingly, envy is closely linked to guilt, a reproach to the self for having done something that could have been done differently, such as cheating on someone we care about, even love.

At some level, envy and guilt involve the sense of responsibility. Aristotle points to the fact that we tend to envy those who are close to us, live in our vicinity, and are of comparable age as well as social status. According to the ancient philosopher, we tend to envy those in whom we can recognize ourselves: “Envy pertains to the idea that we have of ourselves, what makes our difference, our identity, it touches us at our very core.”31 As we can see, envy as emotional spinoff of possession is a concept flying high in putative meaning.

Self–other comparison is what fundamentally underlies both envy and jealousy as psychological phenomena.32 But upstream of such fundamental self–other comparison, there is the feeling experience of possession. In envying others we tend to reproach ourselves with the fact that we do not own something we should have. We are frustrated by the incapacity of owning that same thing. Accordingly, envying is to mourn our own impotency at getting what we could have. In other words, it is the experience of disempowerment. Likewise, in jealousy, the fear of loss or of losing an object of love and devotion, there is the experience of a loss of something felt as owned and over which one had control. Therefore, attached to both envy and jealousy there is the basic feeling experience of entitlement and ownership, hence the feeling of possession.

In jealousy, we basically lose control over a loved one, typically to some rival who is real but often can be imaginary, a mere projection of our deep fear of a loss of control and command over our affective life. In many instances of jealousy drama, the delusion of rivalry is involved, as if the jealous person is objectifying causes to his or her ordeal. Such objectification serves the purpose of bringing some coherence in the chaos of irrationality and awful pain associated with jealous feelings. It is a desperate attempt at fighting pain, at alleviating the excruciating experience of rejection from the loved one, worst of all ordeals. In jealousy, the fear of rejection, mother of all fears, can take extreme forms of wrath, rage, and irrationality. Individuals can lose all judgment and codes of law grant extenuating circumstances to murderers proven to have acted under a jealous spell.

Passion and wrath aside, jealousy is inseparable from the experience of possession, the possession of something differentiated from the self but that one feels entitled to own. As we have seen, possession is the experience of assimilation to the self of things or persons that exist in independence of one’s own body (process of incorporation). This process is in essence symbolic but can be embodied when the object of possession becomes a natural extension of the body as in the case of a tool (e.g., stilts, tennis racket, glasses, jewelry, hammer).

The same applies to envy, which consists in a claim of ownership of something that is missing to the self and needs to be incorporated or self-appropriated. Both entail incorporation, literally the assimilation into the body (embodiment) of external things, whether material (physical object) or immaterial (an idea, a style, a concept). As already mentioned, in many ways the psychological process of incorporation that underlies the experience of possession is analogous to the metabolizing of food by the body that incorporates and processes energy for its survival.

Such a process generalizes to immaterial things like objects of love and fantasies of control and seductive ascendance over people. At a psychological level, external things tend to be assimilated and end up fusing with the self. In a way, jealousy is the fear or the actual experience of the loss of something that ended up belonging to the self. It is the suffering arising from the wrench of someone’s inner being. The fear of losing property and control over someone or something, losing proprietary and ownership “rights” over a lover or a portion of territory. The word “property” comes from the Latin word proprius which stands for “what cannot be shared with others.”

Mundane examples of such remarkable psychological processes abound, most of the time expressed at an unconscious and implicit level of awareness. For example, it appears that many people invest a lot in their cars, both materially and emotionally. They groom them like they groom their own body. Cars are, in most instances, an extension of the self. People can recognize themselves in such material things that they carefully choose and groom. Like shoes and ties, cars are a non-trivial extension of one’s own body. They are experienced as such, notwithstanding the fact that cars in particular do facilitate self-propelled locomotion. They also promote social affiliation by the public display of status and reputation.

Explicit laws aside, and at a basic phenomenal level, the feeling experience of “proprius” or exclusive possession that leads eventually toward envy and jealousy rests on three basic psychological ingredients. These ingredients account for the irrepressible need to incorporate as ours the things that exist essentially in independence of us, be it people or material things like cars, houses, clothes, or land.

The first ingredient is a sense of self, in particular a sense of self as differentiated from objects and other people.33 The idea is simple: in order to incorporate something, the necessary prerequisite is to have something that comes from the outside. In other words, possession experience implies, at the most basic level, a differentiation between self and world: what pertains to the body and what does not. Once this requirement is fulfilled, the second necessary ingredient is the propensity to somehow objectify things and people as differentiated entities, to perceive them as such, and to consider them as objects of contemplation and exploration. This second ingredient is the ability of an individual to project, or eject outward, things that exist in independence of them. Contrary to the Freudian psychoanalytical meaning of projection considered as a major defense mechanism, projection here is considered as the propensity to eject outward and to create objects of thought, contemplation, and desire. Projection, in the sense proposed here, pertains to the objectification of subjective (self-evident) experience that is lived within the body.

But self–world differentiation and projection are not yet sufficient to explain the sense of possession and entitlement we are so inclined to experience, particularly when it becomes explicit (“That’s mine!”). As third ingredient, there is the necessity to identify with the thing differentiated and objectified. Identification is the process of self-recognition in entities that exist outside of one’s own body, entities that are differentiated and objectified.

Accordingly, the feeling of possession, at least in our species so ostentatiously prone to experience envy and jealousy, rests on the articulation and combination of these three basic ingredients. The model can be summarized in a simple equation: 34

SENSE OF OWNERSHIP = DIFFERENTIATION × PROJECTION × IDENTIFICATION

In subsequent chapters pertaining to the developmental origins of possession (Part II), this simple model will be useful in our discussion of how children develop a sense of ownership and entitlement. More importantly, it will be useful when considering the developmental origins of the various ways of relinquishing ownership via negotiation, rather than coercion (see Chapter 2).

If exclusive feelings of possession foster negative emotional spinoffs like envy and jealousy, they are also what afford sharing as the proximate mechanism of group and intergroup harmony.

At a much larger, societal and group level, behind the literal forceful, compulsive, and defensive feeling experiences of possession that are sources of devastating emotions like envy and jealousy, lies also – paradoxically at first sight – the seed of social harmony. The essentially selfish feeling of possession and the forceful appropriation of things to the self is the necessary counterpart of all the intricate pro-social ways, including institutions we have evolved to promote peace, cooperation, communal empathy, and social stability.

In humans, and possibly also in some other nonhuman primate species,35 affiliation is promoted when shared feelings of possession become the bargaining chips of social peace. This is evident in the case of gift exchanges, when dispossession becomes voluntary and ritualized to promote social bonding. 36

It is reasonable to view the experience of possession as the bottom-line engine of pro-social morality, in the same way that all economists could claim that possession and consumerism are the necessary conditions of any exchange system. In other words, without the feeling of possession, there would be no morality, just as there would be no economy.

Possession and morality

Controlling and feeling control over things such as food, progeny, territory, loved ones, or sexual partner is de facto the necessary prerequisite of any creatures living in an environment where resources are scarce and competition is high. Social animals are under the permanent threat of losing what is under their control, including their own life. Morality, as explicit or implicit systems of social norms, evolved to regulate the basic propensity to possess, particularly potential conflicts over possession.

To survive as groups, each social species evolved particular buffers to alleviate inescapable conflicts over possession, preventing group extinction and mutual extermination. These buffering systems are necessary to bring harmonious group equilibrium, assuring some perpetuity of the species. In humans, these systems are incarnated in moral institutions like tribunals, books of laws, explicit legal codes, constitutions, etc., but also implicit social rules, tacit know-hows and “etiquettes” transmitted from generation to generation as ways of ruling conflicts and regulating group dynamic.

But each social species has evolved its own particular and complex ways of regulating inter-individual competition and conflicts, with tacit principles and inclinations such as cooperation (helping and collaboration), reconciliation (peace making), first possession (deference to first possessor), tit-for-tat exchanges (I give because you give me), or reciprocal altruism (I give because you gave me).

Morality emerged in humans, and also in other primate species,37 primarily as a system of social rules and norms evolved to regulate recurrent conflicts over possession. One is hard pressed to conceive morality in independence of possession and conflicts necessarily arising from it because of competition over scarce resources.

There is biblical evidence of this predicament when we consider that six of the Ten Commandments in the Old Testament pertain to issues of putative conflict over possession regarding object, life, wife, body, or truth.38 There is also ontogenetic evidence for such an assertion, as issues of ethics or codes of conduct arise first and foremost in the context of fights over possession: “That’s mine!,” “I want one too!,” “Give it back!,” “It’s not yours!,” etc. First social conflicts and rivalry tensions over possession are well documented from the end of the second year, when children become explicit claimers of what is theirs.39 It is primarily in such conflict and rivalry contexts that adults are constrained to come up with explicit “deontic” rules of dos and don’ts. In such interventions aimed at fostering peace, children are exposed to the rulings and moral ways of their social niche. They will eventually internalize and transmit such cultural models to future generations. This is another, simple way of stating that the feeling of possession is a necessary precursor, the experiential prerequisite for the evolution of any implicit or explicit ruling meant to promote social harmony, whether such a system rests on simple alliance, tit-for-tat exchanges, basic empathy, or higher-order explicit cultural and symbolic systems like the Ten Commandments.

Further evidence of the link between possession and moral obligations is once again evident in the pioneer works of early anthropologists like Marcel Mauss (1872–1950) and Bronislaw Malinowski (1884–1942). In the early twentieth century, these anthropologists established that gift systems or ceremonials of relinquishing possession are cardinal cultural institutions among pre-industrial societies from all latitudes. Gift systems are universal, identified as the cornerstone of social harmony within and between indigenous “primitive” human groups. The pioneer ethnographic works of Mauss and Malinowski, among many others,40 demonstrate that, in human evolution, implicit feeling experience of possession is transformed into explicit and ritualized (symbolic) relinquishing of possession as “gift,” within complex exchange practices fostering long-term harmonious inter-individual and inter-group relations via social debts and the strict obligation to reciprocate in an endless circularity of gift giving (e.g., the Kula circle described by Malinowski in the Solomon Islands of Melanesia).

If possession governs the social lives of all animals, in humans the experience of possession has unique features. If it shares crucial roots and aspects that are unquestionably homologous to those expressed in fish, birds, and all mammals, as in the case of the defense of progeny and territory, it is not strictly comparable. We belong to a species that is self-conscious, and particularly prone to caring about reputation. In this context, we develop a psychology and feeling experience of possession that has some unique if not awkward features, namely symbolic spinoffs not found in other animals (see Chapter 4). Among such spinoffs are humans’ irrepressible animistic and fetishistic tendencies toward objects, projecting vitality into things and leading us to worship cult objects.41 Such highly symbolic worshiping is not a trivial feature of the human psyche since it has recurrently led us to kill each other. We are taught that Christian Crusades were aimed at regaining possession of the Holy Sepulcher in Jerusalem, the tomb of Christ: the reason for hundreds of thousands of deaths. In the meantime, as symbolic counterpart, we have also evolved cultural institutions like the International Tribunal at The Hague and the United Nations.

Other animals have also evolved complex ways and practices to promote social harmony and contain their forceful possession psychology (e.g., dominance hierarchy, alliances, instinctive regulation of aggression and defensiveness).42 But unlike humans, this sedimentation of pro-social norms is not symbolic and not imbued with human beings’ more often than not weird symbolic spinoffs, evident in fetishism, superstitions, and other animistic propensities. These are ontologically different.

Like any other social animal, we respond to threats of being dispossessed and losing control over possessions as if it were an attack on our own body. But in humans, it is often highly symbolic and abstract, removed from literal signals or signifiers to which other animals tend to respond automatically or in a predictable, conditioned manner. The reasons for human defensive aggression over possession are often far removed from the actual, literal situation. It tends easily to take some unpredictable irrational spinoffs with no obvious underlying adaptive reasons. We might resort to psychoanalytical concepts and other sublimation processes to account for them. How can we otherwise make sense of road rage and people pulling guns for a scratch on their car as if it was an integral part of their embodied self? How to make sense of devastating human crusades around sacred sepulchers and other sanctified objects? How to explain terrorist acts and other jihads pronounced against novelists or caricaturists for their ideas and ideological transgressions? How can the lives of young soldiers be so readily sacrificed for pieces of land that often are not even strategic but stand as purely symbolic in relation to elusive religious or political beliefs?

1 This is particularly evident in Albert Michotte’s classic demonstrations of perceived causality in dynamic events involving inanimate protagonists that we irrepressibly perceive as “agents and patients” of intentional actions (Michotte, The Perception of Causality). The same is evident in Heider and Simmel’s pioneer demonstration of the obligatory inference of intentions that we tend to engage in automatically, trying to make sense of dynamic displays that involve the relative motion of geometric figures like squares and triangles that are compulsively described by viewers as “chasing each other and escaping one another,” an unmistakable sign of higher-order projection (Heider and Simmel, “An experimental study of apparent behaviour”).

2 See John Searle’s famous Chinese room thought experiment for a thorough discussion of the limits of machine simulation, and the extent to which machines can equate human intelligence, in particular higher-level competence like language. The conclusion is that comparable performance does not necessarily entail comparable competence. A machine can only perform in comparable ways, it cannot speak as such.

Moral Acrobatics How We Avoid Ethical Ambiguity by Thinking in Black and White, Oxford University Press 2021. Kindle Edition.

Moral Acrobatics: How We Avoid Ethical Ambiguity by Thinking in Black and White 1st Edition, Kindle Edition, [CDN$ 19.19], Oxford University Press; 1st edition (Dec 18 2020) ASIN: B08QW5S8J3, Page numbers source ISBN: 0190057653

Philippe Rochat is Professor of Psychology at Emory University. He received his PhD from the University of Geneva, and studied infants as a pre-doctoral and post-doctoral fellow at Brown University, the University of Pennsylvania, and Johns Hopkins University. A 2006-2007 John Simon Guggenheim fellow, he has written over one hundred scholarly articles and is the single author of five books, as well as the editor or co-editor of three books

Although it is difficult for us to fathom, pure monsters do not exist. Terrorists and other serial killers massacre innocent people, yet are perfectly capable of loving their own parents, neighbors, and children. Hitler, sending millions to their death, was contemptuous of meat eaters and a strong advocate of animal welfare. How do we reconcile such moral ambiguities? Do they capture something deep about how we build values? As a developmental scientist, Philippe Rochat explores this possibility, proposing that as members of a uniquely symbolic and self-conscious species aware of its own mortality, we develop uncanny abilities toward lying and self-deception. We are deeply categorical and compartmentalized in our views of the world. We imagine essence where there is none. We juggle double standards and manage contradictory values, clustering our existence depending on context and situations, whether we deal in relation to close kin, colleagues, strangers, lovers, or enemies. We live within multiple, interchangeable moral spheres. This social-contextual determination of the moral domain is the source of moral ambiguities and blatant contradictions we all need to own up to.
